extracted.intended_audience: general readers interested in literature, social criticism, and commentary on contemporary (late-19th-century) life
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying standards for judging fiction and prose style (truth vs escapism, characterization, pathos, humour) and commentary on the relevance of traditional military drill. Targets both how to assess literature and how to judge appropriateness of military training methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modern military training should aim at individual sense not combined solidity
rubrics_metrics.description: “Now, when we shoot from behind cover with smokeless powder, brain not brute force—individual sense not combined solidity is surely the result to be aimed at.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument that under modern warfare conditions the emphasis should shift from collective drill formations to the individual soldier’s judgement and initiative. The author contrasts medieval/earlier massed combat (where precise combined movement mattered) with contemporary skirmishing from cover, using this as a standard for evaluating the usefulness of drill and training methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drill sergeant’s role is antiquated
rubrics_metrics.description: “the proper place for the drill sergeant nowadays is under a glass case in some museum of antiquities.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used as an evaluative claim: the traditional drill-sergeant model is portrayed as outdated and ill-matched to modern warfare. Illustrated with anecdotes (Hyde Park barracks, the dog Columbus) showing the mismatch between ritualized shouting/drill and practical effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Politeness and tailored instruction work better than shouting
rubrics_metrics.description: The Albany Barracks anecdote where the sergeant abandons shouting and adopts a deferential, social tone: “Good morning, gentlemen... well, now, gentlemen, what do you say to falling in?”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides how instruction should be adapted to the audience: calm, respectful, and individualised correction can achieve compliance and better morale among non-typical recruits. Examples include gentle, specific corrections (e.g., 'a little further forward, number three') and humorous, human approaches that still achieve the drill’s ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Uniformity is safe but monotonous
rubrics_metrics.description: “Believe me, gentlemen, this thing has been carefully worked out, and no improvement is likely to result from individual effort. Let our idea be uniformity. It is monotonous, but it is safe.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expresses the military standard valuing uniformity as a conservative safety measure; useful as a criterion to weigh against the earlier call for individual initiative. The text frames this as a legitimate trade-off (safety and simplicity vs adaptability and initiative).

rubrics_metrics.name: Literature’s dual purposes: escapism (fairyland) vs moral/truthful reflection
rubrics_metrics.description: “Should a novel or play call us to ponder upon the problems of existence, or lure us ... into the pleasant meadows of dreamland?... If only the latter, then let our heroes and our heroines be not what men and women are, but what they should be.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides two competing evaluative modes for fiction: (a) imaginative escapism where characters are idealized and plots reassure, and (b) serious literature that confronts reality and provokes thought. The author endorses that both branches are needful, and this distinction can be used to judge a work according to its aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: To be a living force, literature must deal with all sides of life
rubrics_metrics.description: “If literature is to be a help to us, as well as a pastime, it must deal with the ugly as well as with the beautiful; it must show us ourselves, not as we wish to appear, but as we know ourselves to be.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Asserts a normative standard for literature intended to inform or help: authenticity and inclusion of life’s uglier aspects are virtues. Cites Dickens and Zola as examples of writers occupying different but valuable places on this axis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Books that live are plain tales simply told
rubrics_metrics.description: “To sum up, ‘David Copperfield’ is a plain tale, simply told; and such are all books that live.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims stylistic simplicity and straightforward storytelling are key to longevity and popular endurance. Warns that eccentricities of style and artistic trickery may please critics of the day but do not guarantee a work will endure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid bathos by careful handling of pathos
rubrics_metrics.description: “Too often his pathos sinks to bathos, and this not from want of skill, but from want of care.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative rule for dramatic/emotional writing: pathos must be crafted with restraint and care to avoid sliding into bathos (unintended, excessive sentimentality). Examples: contrasts Dickens’ less successful sentimental deaths (Paul Dombey, Little Nell) with more restrained, effective scenes (Barkis, Sidney Carton).

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization: types vs full characters
rubrics_metrics.description: “In Uriah Heap and Mrs. Gummidge, Dickens draws types rather than characters.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offers a criterion for evaluating character-drawing: distinguishing between typified personifications of human characteristics (effective for satire or moral emphasis) and fully rounded, realistic characters. The author lists many Dickens figures as examples of 'types' and notes both the utility and limits of this approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour does not preclude literary merit
rubrics_metrics.description: “’Huck Finn’ would be a great work were there not a laugh in it from cover to cover.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pushes back against a critical bias that treats humour as incompatible with serious literature. Use this as a defense of comic works’ artistic worth (Mark Twain cited), and as a caution against critical fashions that equate solemnity with value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faithfulness to life is not the sole key to commercial success
rubrics_metrics.description: “If faithfulness to life were the key to literary success, Gissing’s sales would have been counted by the million instead of by the hundred.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An observation to temper critical expectations: fidelity to realism or 'truthfulness to life' does not guarantee popular or financial success. Use when evaluating the relationship between artistic virtues and reception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Idealisation of women reduces realism in fiction
rubrics_metrics.description: “Dickens’ good women are all too good for human nature’s daily food... Scott’s women were likewise mere illuminated texts.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical criterion about representation: excessively idealized female characters (pure, faultless women) weaken a work’s realism. The author contrasts instances of convincing female characterisation (Bella Wilfer, Estella, Catherine Seton) with more formulaic depictions, recommending more lifelike portrayals for authenticity.
